description: IoT Village at DEF CON 25 explores security vulnerabilities in connected devices and emerging threats from botnets to medical devices. The 15 talks cover IoT attack vectors, defensive techniques, policy implications, and hardware security research.

talks.title: The call is coming from inside the house
talks.teaser: The second half of 2016 saw the rise of a new generation of IoT botnets consisting of webcams and other IoT devices. These botnets were then subsequently used to launch DDoS attacks on an unprecedented scale against O...
talks.summary:
### The Watershed Rise of IoT Botnets
At 00:00, Steinthor Bjarnason and Jason Jones of Arbor Networks open by contextualizing the massive shift in Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks that occurred in late 2016. The sudden emergence of IoT-based botnets—most notably Mirai, alongside precursors and variants like Hajime and Leash—shattered previous traffic volume records. Botnets consisting of hundreds of thousands of compromised embedded devices launched terabit-scale floods against KrebsOnSecurity, hosting provider OVH, and DNS backbone provider Dyn.

### Anatomy of the Mirai Scanner and Propagation Engine
At 06:12 and 11:45, the speakers dissect the source code and operational architecture of Mirai. Unlike traditional PC malware that relies on complex software exploits, Mirai achieved unprecedented scale through simplicity. The malware continuously executed high-frequency SYN scanning across IPv4 address space on TCP ports 23 (Telnet) and 2323. Upon discovering an open listener, it initiated automated brute-force attacks against a hardcoded dictionary containing just 62 default username and password combinations commonly hardcoded into CCTV cameras, digital video recorders (DVRs), and residential routers.

### Command-and-Control Infrastructure and Attack Vectors
At 18:16, the presentation analyzes Mirai's command-and-control (C2) protocols and traffic generation mechanisms. Once recruited, bots received encrypted binary instructions to execute synchronized volumetric reflection attacks, including DNS amplification, SYN floods, ACK floods, and specialized GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) floods. Because embedded Linux systems generate line-rate network traffic with zero user productivity impact, compromised devices sustained high-bandwidth packet floods indefinitely without owners noticing device degradation.

### "The Call is Coming from Inside the House"
At 24:30 and 29:15, Bjarnason and Jones explore the alarming operational reality that gave the presentation its title: infected IoT devices reside within residential subscriber networks behind consumer NAT routers. Internet Service Providers (ISPs) faced massive internal outbound packet floods, causing residential DSL and fiber aggregation routers to buckle under state-table exhaustion. The authors highlight how lack of BCP 38 ingress filtering allowed bots to spoof source IP addresses, turning consumer access networks into weaponized attack launchpads.

### Mitigating IoT Botnets and Coordinated Defenses
Concluding from 32:00 to 34:59, the authors outline collaborative industry defense frameworks. They advocate for automated ISP edge filtering, proactive consumer device quarantine, and the enforcement of BCP 38 source address validation across transit providers. Furthermore, they call for strict IoT manufacturing standards, including mandatory unique device passwords and automated firmware patching, to eradicate the pervasive insecure default configurations fueling global botnet proliferation.

talks.teaser: Get out your rollerblades, plug in your camo keyboard, and fire up your BLT drive. It's 25 years later and we're still hacking the planet. The Exploitee.rs are back with new 0day, new exploits and more fun. Celebratin...
talks.summary:
### The Exploitee.rs Hardware Hacking Showcase
At 00:00, the Exploitee.rs research team (Zenofex, 0x00string, CJ 000, and Maximus64) takes the stage for a high-energy presentation demonstrating zero-day exploitation across mainstream Internet of Things (IoT) consumer devices. Celebrating DEF CON's 25th anniversary, the team emphasizes their commitment to publishing full exploit toolkits, hardware pinouts, and technical documentation to advance independent consumer security research.

### Western Digital My Cloud NAS Remote Command Execution
At 08:30 and 16:15, the team breaks down their investigation of the Western Digital My Cloud Network Attached Storage (NAS) platform. By reverse-engineering the device's web server binaries and PHP administration scripts, they uncovered multiple unauthenticated command injection vulnerabilities. They demonstrate chaining an unauthenticated cookie bypass with arbitrary command execution, allowing a remote attacker on the local network—or via cross-site request forgery (CSRF)—to achieve root privileges and exfiltrate private storage volumes without providing credentials.

### ASUSTOR NAS System Compromise
At 23:40, the presenters shift focus to ASUSTOR commercial storage appliances. They detail how vulnerabilities in the device's administrative web portal allow attackers to bypass login validation through improper input sanitization in system configuration scripts. The team demonstrates a fully automated remote root shell exploit, illustrating how common design flaws plague enterprise-grade storage hardware.

### Smart Home Hubs and Media Streaming Devices
At 30:28 and 38:50, the team explores vulnerabilities within smart home controllers and media streaming devices. They walk through hardware reverse engineering steps: desoldering SPI flash memory chips, locating hidden UART and JTAG debug headers on printed circuit boards, and extracting raw filesystem partitions using Binwalk. They reveal how unencrypted local API endpoints and insecure firmware validation routines allow persistent hardware backdoors to be flashed onto smart hubs.

### Practical Remediation and Open Research
Concluding between 48:10 and 59:21, the Exploitee.rs team releases their open-source exploit scripts and hardware write-ups on `exploitee.rs`. They issue a strong critique of consumer electronics manufacturers who ignore vulnerability disclosures, treat hardware security as an afterthought, and ship devices with obsolete Linux kernels. They urge consumers and researchers to demand transparent patching and hardware auditability from device vendors.

talks.title: IoT  From DVRs to Dildos
talks.summary:
### Expanding IoT Vulnerabilities Beyond Mirai
At 00:00, Andrew Tierney and Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners open with a critique of post-Mirai security discussions. While the industry became fixated on simple default Telnet credentials, the speakers emphasize that commercial IoT security remains fundamentally broken across much deeper architectural layers: insecure Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) implementations, unprotected local API endpoints, unencrypted mobile app telemetry, and flawed cloud backend integrations.

### Reverse Engineering Smart Adult Devices
At 06:12 and 12:40, the speakers explore their vulnerability research into internet-connected and Bluetooth-controlled adult novelty devices (including smart vibrators and remote chastity cages). They demonstrate that consumer products handling exceptionally intimate personal data frequently feature negligible security engineering. Teardowns revealed that many devices broadcast predictable BLE advertisements without pairing authentication, allowing anyone within radio range to intercept telemetry, hijack motor controls, or track device usage patterns.

### Eavesdropping on Intimate Sensor Telemetry
At 18:05, Tierney shares case studies where adult toys incorporated integrated temperature sensors, accelerometers, and live audio chat features. Due to lack of Transport Layer Security (TLS) and insecure cloud storage buckets, live audio streams, usage timestamps, and battery telemetry were transmitted unencrypted across the Internet. An eavesdropper on the same Wi-Fi network could intercept private audio recordings and reconstruct intimate personal habits in real time.

### Insecure Cloud APIs and Account Takeover
At 24:50 and 30:15, Munro dissects the web APIs that support mobile companion applications. The team identified pervasive Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerabilities, missing rate limits, and unauthenticated API endpoints that allowed researchers to enumerate user accounts, access registered email addresses and location logs, and send remote control commands to arbitrary devices worldwide without authorization.

### Ethics, Intimate Privacy, and Responsible Disclosure
Concluding from 33:10 to 36:19, the presenters discuss the complex ethical and privacy considerations unique to adult IoT technology. They recount the frustrating experience of attempting responsible vulnerability disclosures to vendors who lack security contact channels or deny liability. Munro and Tierney argue that because intimate IoT devices present genuine physical, emotional, and privacy risks, researchers must aggressively hold manufacturers accountable to baseline data protection standards.

talks.title: Hide Yo Keys,  Hide Yo Car
talks.teaser: Today, most vehicle manufacturers in the US connect their vehicles to a type of network and delegate controls to mobile or web applications upon vehicle purchasing. Thankfully, security research for consumer devices a...
talks.summary:
### Connected Vehicles and the Expanding Mobile Attack Surface
At 00:00, Aaron Guzman opens by exploring the intersection of modern automotive technology and consumer telematics. Major automobile manufacturers increasingly integrate cellular modems into vehicles, delegating critical operations—such as door unlocking, horn sounding, GPS tracking, and remote engine ignition—to consumer smartphone applications and cloud telematics portals. Guzman argues that while researchers have extensively examined CAN bus vulnerabilities, mobile API integrations represent a widely accessible, low-friction attack surface.

### Anatomy of Automotive Telematics Portals
At 05:30 and 11:15, Guzman details his security audit of the Subaru Starlink telematics ecosystem and its supporting mobile application. He deconstructs the application architecture, which communicates with third-party telematics service providers via RESTful web APIs. By routing mobile app traffic through an intercepting HTTP proxy (Burp Suite), he analyzes JSON request payloads, authentication headers, session management, and API authorization checks.

### Exploiting Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR)
At 18:14, the presentation details the discovery of severe authorization bypasses and Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerabilities within the telematics API. Guzman shows that when issuing commands to locate or unlock a vehicle, the API trusted arbitrary client-supplied vehicle identification parameters without verifying whether the authenticated user was the registered vehicle owner. Furthermore, API response tokens and session credentials were improperly cached across client instances.

### Remote Vehicle Actuation and GPS Location Tracking
At 24:30 and 29:45, Guzman demonstrates the practical real-world impact of these API vulnerabilities. An unprivileged attacker with knowledge of a target's VIN or account identifier could issue API requests to remotely locate a vehicle via GPS, unlock the doors, sound the panic horn, and remotely start the engine. Because these commands traverse cellular infrastructure directly to the vehicle's onboard telematics unit, attacks could be executed silently from anywhere in the world without physical proximity.

### Telematics API Hardening and Vendor Remediation
Concluding between 31:40 and 34:50, Guzman reviews the responsible disclosure process with Subaru and their backend telematics vendors. He details the remediation steps implemented, including robust server-side authorization enforcement, short-lived session tokens, API rate-limiting, and eliminating sensitive data leakage in response headers. He emphasizes that automotive manufacturers must treat connected mobile APIs with the same rigorous defense-in-depth applied to powertrain safety controls.

talks.title: The Internet of Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: The “Internet of Things” (IoT) is taking over our lives, so we should be constantly questioning the security and integrity of these technologies. As an IoT researcher, this is precisely what I do. During this presenta...
talks.summary:
### The Multi-Layered IoT Threat Landscape
At 00:00, Deral Heiland, IoT Research Lead at Rapid7, introduces his comprehensive methodology for auditing the "Internet of Vulnerabilities." He emphasizes that assessing IoT security requires looking beyond individual devices: a true IoT ecosystem spans four interconnected attack surfaces: physical hardware interfaces, embedded firmware, local RF communication protocols, and cloud/mobile application infrastructure.

### Physical Hardware Reconnaissance and Firmware Extraction
At 06:45 and 13:20, Heiland covers physical hardware auditing techniques. He demonstrates identifying test pads and debug headers on printed circuit boards using multimeters and logic analyzers to discover active UART consoles and JTAG interfaces. He walks through dumping raw flash memory chips (both SPI flash and NAND flash) and employing tools like Binwalk to unpack file systems, recover hardcoded root credentials, and identify unpatched Linux daemons and proprietary binaries.

### Radio Protocol Sniffing: Zigbee, Z-Wave, and BLE
At 18:35, the presentation shifts to wireless protocols connecting smart home peripherals. Heiland discusses auditing Zigbee and Z-Wave networks using Software Defined Radios (SDR) and dedicated transceivers (such as the KillerBee framework). He explains how improper key exchange procedures during initial network joining allow nearby eavesdroppers to capture the default network transport key and decrypt smart lock, lighting, and sensor communications over the air.

### Cloud API Parameter Tampering and Mass Data Exposure
At 22:53, Heiland highlights severe architectural flaws in IoT cloud companion APIs. He illustrates how insecure API pagination allows trivial data harvesting: by tampering with request parameters—such as setting the query offset to one and the record limit to one million—an unauthenticated user could extract the entire customer database, complete with GPS coordinates, user account credentials, and device telemetry.

### Structuring Enterprise IoT Audits
Concluding between 35:10 and 47:04, Heiland provides actionable guidance for enterprise organizations deploying or manufacturing IoT solutions. He stresses the necessity of eliminating hardware debug ports on production boards, enforcing cryptographic signature validation on firmware images, encrypting radio communication keys at rest, and conducting rigorous API penetration tests prior to product deployment.

talks.title: Redesigning PKI For IoT Because Crypto is Hard
talks.teaser: As the previous Director of Security at companies like Linksys, Belkin, and Wink, I learned hard lessons about the pitfalls of PKI. This was especially true on IoT devices, where the responsibility was on consumers or...
talks.summary:
### The Reality of PKI in Constrained IoT Hardware
At 00:00, Brian Knopf reflects on his tenure as Director of Security at major consumer hardware manufacturers including Linksys, Belkin, and Wink. He introduces the central dilemma of connected device security: while Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is widely heralded as the gold standard for authentication and encryption, implementing traditional enterprise PKI on cost-constrained, resource-limited IoT hardware is exceptionally difficult and fraught with implementation pitfalls.

### Common Cryptographic Pitfalls in Mass Production
At 08:15 and 15:30, Knopf outlines the most prevalent cryptographic mistakes made by consumer electronics manufacturers. Constrained devices frequently lack hardware Real-Time Clocks (RTCs), meaning devices boot with clocks set to the Unix epoch or build dates, causing immediate TLS certificate expiration validation failures. Furthermore, manufacturers routinely hardcode identical private keys across entire product lines in unencrypted SPI flash memory or predictable filesystem paths, allowing an attacker who extracts one key to compromise millions of devices.

### The Broken State of Certificate Revocation
At 22:44, the speaker examines the near-total failure of standard certificate revocation mechanisms on embedded devices. Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) quickly grow too large to fit in limited device RAM, while Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) requests fail when devices operate behind strict enterprise firewalls or suffer intermittent internet connectivity. When a private key is leaked in production, IoT vendors find themselves incapable of revoking trust without permanently bricking deployed hardware.

### Hardware Roots of Trust and Secure Elements
At 30:10 and 36:40, Knopf advocates for integrating hardware-based roots of trust into IoT bill-of-materials. He explains how low-cost crypto coprocessors, Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs), and secure elements (such as Microchip ATECC chips) allow private keys to be generated and stored securely on silicon, preventing key extraction via bus sniffing or flash dumping. He emphasizes that unique, per-device asymmetric certificates must be injected during factory provisioning.

### Designing Resilient, Manageable IoT PKI Architectures
Concluding from 39:20 to 43:57, Knopf presents architectural blueprints for modern IoT PKI. He recommends deploying dedicated device certificate authorities (CAs), implementing automated certificate renewal protocols, decoupling cryptographic validation from static system clocks, and establishing secure over-the-air firmware recovery pipelines so that security teams can rotate root certificates without disrupting critical consumer services.

talks.title: IIDS: IDS FOR IOT
speakers: Vivek Ramachandran,  Nishant Sharma, Ashish Bhangale
talks.teaser: We all know how vulnerable IoT devices are - but do we know if our home or industrial IoT devices are being attacked or already compromised? This talk focuses on creating an Intrusion Detection System for IoT devices ...
talks.summary:
### The Need for Dedicated IoT Intrusion Detection
At 00:00, Vivek Ramachandran, Nishant Sharma, and Ashish Bhangale open by addressing a critical operational dilemma in smart environments: while security researchers continuously demonstrate that Internet of Things (IoT) devices are vulnerable to compromise, enterprise and consumer networks lack visibility into whether devices are currently under active attack or recruited into botnets. Standard IT intrusion detection systems (IDS) fail to monitor non-IP protocols, creating severe blind spots across wireless sensor networks.

### Multi-Protocol Wireless Monitoring Architecture
At 06:40 and 12:15, the presenters outline the architecture of IIDS (IoT Intrusion Detection System). Rather than relying solely on traditional wired Ethernet tap points, IIDS incorporates multi-radio monitoring hardware capable of simultaneously capturing 802.11 Wi-Fi, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), and Zigbee radio packets. By implementing intelligent, synchronized channel-hopping routines (discussed at 19:54), the sensor array monitors diverse frequency bands without missing sporadic communication bursts from low-power peripherals.

### Anomaly Detection and Attack Signatures
At 23:30, the speakers detail the hybrid detection engine driving IIDS, combining deterministic signature matching with behavioral baseline heuristics. They explain how the system detects common wireless attacks, including 802.11 deauthentication floods, rogue access points spoofing smart home gateways, BLE connection interception, and unauthorized GATT attribute manipulation. On the IP layer, the engine flags anomalous device behaviors, such as a smart thermostat initiating outbound Telnet connections or flooding arbitrary external IPs with high-rate UDP packets.

### Automated Mitigation and Containment
At 32:10 and 40:09, the presentation addresses automated threat response. When a compromise is confirmed, IIDS can trigger active mitigation workflows: transmitting targeted wireless deauthentication frames to disconnect malicious rogue devices, instructing upstream software-defined switches to isolate compromised IP endpoints into quarantine VLANs, or alerting system administrators via mobile notifications before compromised nodes can participate in volumetric DDoS floods.

### Scalable Deployment and Future Roadmap
Concluding the session, the authors demonstrate live detection of an IoT botnet recruitment attempt against smart bulbs and cameras. They discuss open-source hardware reference designs for deploying lightweight IIDS sensor nodes across commercial buildings and industrial campuses, urging organizations to prioritize visibility across RF and embedded protocols as physical infrastructure becomes increasingly digitized.

talks.title: Controlling IoT devices with crafted radio signals
talks.teaser: In this talk, we'll be exploring how wireless communication works. We'll capture digital data live (with Software-Defined Radio), and see how the actual bits are transmitted. From here, we'll see how to view, listen t...
talks.summary:
### The Physical Mechanics of Wireless Transmission
At 00:00, Caleb Madrigal opens with a hands-on exploration of the physical layer in consumer wireless communication. Rather than treating radio signals as abstract network packets, Madrigal emphasizes that all digital wireless signals are simply analog electromagnetic waves modulated to represent binary ones and zeros. By understanding modulation at the physical layer, security researchers can reverse-engineer and manipulate wireless devices without requiring proprietary documentation.

### Signal Capture and Spectrum Characterization
At 05:20 and 10:15, Madrigal demonstrates capturing over-the-air signals from commercial 315 MHz and 433 MHz smart home RF remotes using an inexpensive RTL-SDR receiver paired with GQRX. He exports the raw radio frequency recordings into Audacity to visually inspect the waveform in the time domain. Madrigal explains Amplitude Shift Keying (ASK) and On-Off Keying (OOK), demonstrating how the presence or absence of a carrier wave corresponds directly to digital pulses.

### Reverse Engineering Binary Frames and Pulse Timings
At 16:47, the speaker dives into packet framing and timing analysis. By measuring the microsecond duration of high and low pulses in the captured audio waveform, he uncovers the device's encoding scheme. He breaks down the preamble sync pulses, the unique 20-bit device identification code hardcoded into the remote, and the specific functional command bits assigned to toggle relay switches on and off.

### Crafting and Transmitting Exploitation Signals
At 22:30 and 27:10, Madrigal transitions from passive reception to active signal injection. Using Python scripts and Software-Defined Radio hardware (such as HackRF and Yard Stick One), he synthesizes the precise timing pulses calculated during reverse engineering. He demonstrates transmitting custom RF signals to reliably actuate wireless power outlets across the room, highlighting that the target devices lack rolling codes, replay protection, or cryptographic authentication.

### Demystifying SDR for the Hacker Community
Concluding around 31:57, Madrigal encourages attendees to overcome their intimidation of Software-Defined Radio. He points out that basic sub-GHz radio reverse engineering requires only accessible math, curiosity, and open-source tooling. By viewing the electromagnetic spectrum as an open software canvas, security enthusiasts can audit the security of millions of unencrypted smart devices deployed throughout everyday environments.
